'''Vadim L'vovich Berezinskii''' (July 15, 1935, in Kiev – June 23, 1980, in Moscow)<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Abrikosov|first=A A|last2=Gor'kov|first2=L P|last3=Dzyaloshinskiĭ|first3=I E|last4=Larkin|first4=A I|last5=Migdal|first5=A B|last6=Pitaevskiĭ|first6=Lev P|author-link6=Lev Pitaevskii|last7=Khalatnikov|first7=I M|date=1981|title=Vadim L'vovich Berezinskiĭ (Obituary)|journal=Soviet Physics Uspekhi|language=en|volume=24|issue=3|pages=249–250|doi=10.1070/PU1981v024n03ABEH004788|issn=0038-5670}}</ref> was a Soviet physicist.

He was born in Kiev and graduated from [[Moscow State University]] in 1959. He then worked in Moscow and the [[Landau Institute for Theoretical Physics]]. He is notable for having identified the role played by topological defects in the low-temperature phase of two-dimensional systems with a continuous symmetry.<ref>V. L. Berezinskii, Destruction of long-range order in one-dimensional and two-dimensional systems having a continuous symmetry group I, Classical systems. Sov. Phys. JETP, '''32''', 493 (1971)</ref><ref>V. L. Berezinskii, Destruction of long-range order in one-dimensional and two-dimensional systems possessing a continuous symmetry group II, Quantum systems, Sov. Phys. JETP '''34''', 610 (1972).</ref> His work led to the discovery of the [[Kosterlitz–Thouless transition|Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition]], for which [[John M. Kosterlitz]] and [[David J. Thouless]] were awarded the Nobel Prize in 2016. He also developed a technique for treating electrons in one-dimensional disordered systems and provided first consistent proof of one-dimensional localization,<ref>V. L. Berezinskii, Kinetics of a quantum particle in a one-dimensional random potential, Sov. Phys. JETP '''38''', 620 (1974)</ref> and predicted negative-gap superconductivity.<ref>V. L. Berezinskii, New model of the anisotropic phase of superfluid 
He³, JETP Lett. '''20''', 287 (1974) </ref>
